paragraphs.heading: Sensors and alarms
paragraphs.text: A tsunami warning system detects a tsunami ahead of time and issues warnings to save lives and limit damage to property. It has two parts that matter equally: a network of sensors that spots tsunamis, and a communications network that sends out alarms quickly enough for people to evacuate the coast. Such systems come in two kinds, international and regional.

paragraphs.heading: Racing the wave
paragraphs.text: An earthquake alert triggers the first watches and warnings. Then sea level readings, from tide gauges on shore or from DART buoys, confirm whether a tsunami really exists. The approach works because an earthquake's seismic waves travel at about 4 km/s, so a quake is picked up almost at once, while a tsunami in open water moves at 500 to 1,000 km/h. That leaves time to make a forecast and warn threatened areas if needed. But the link between earthquakes and tsunamis is not fully understood, so the reliability of these systems is limited.

paragraphs.heading: Lessons from the Pacific
paragraphs.text: The first rough attempt at a tsunami alert was made in Hawaii in the 1920s. Better systems followed two tsunamis that devastated Hilo, Hawaii, in 1946 and 1960, the first from an Aleutian Islands earthquake and the second from the Valdivia earthquake. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center was set up in 1949, after the 1946 tsunami caused 165 casualties in Hawaii and Alaska. Run by the US agency NOAA from Ewa Beach, Hawaii, it issues warnings for most of the Pacific, while NOAA's National Tsunami Warning Center in Palmer, Alaska, founded in 1967, covers North America.

paragraphs.heading: Gaps in the Indian Ocean
paragraphs.text: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed almost 250,000 people. In January 2005 a United Nations conference in Kobe, Japan, decided the UN should set up an Indian Ocean warning system, which led to a system for Indonesia and other affected areas. Indonesia's system fell out of use in 2012 when its detection buoys stopped working, leaving only seismic detection and no way to predict tsunamis caused by volcanic eruptions. Indonesia was struck by tsunamis in September and December 2018, the second caused by a volcano, and the government then installed sea level sensors to fill the gap.

paragraphs.heading: Fast local warnings
paragraphs.text: Regional or local centres use seismic data on nearby quakes to judge whether a local tsunami is possible. They can warn the public through loudspeakers and sirens in less than 15 minutes. The location and size of an undersea quake and the likely arrival times can be worked out fast, but it is almost always impossible to know whether the sea floor has shifted in a way that will make tsunami waves. So false alarms happen, yet they cause little disruption, because these quick warnings cover only a small area, while a real tsunami would hit much more.

paragraphs.heading: Japan and India
paragraphs.text: Japan runs a nationwide system that usually issues a tsunami warning minutes after an Earthquake Early Warning, if waves are expected. During the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake it issued a warning within 3 minutes at its most serious level, a major tsunami, meaning waves at least 3 m high. An improved system was unveiled on 7 March 2013. After the 2004 tsunami struck its coasts, India set up INCOIS, the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, in Hyderabad, which offers tsunami warnings along with ocean forecasts and fishing zone advice.
